analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from forcing consumers into binding arbitration in standard contracts.
analysis.headline: The Consumer Fairness Act of 1999 never received a committee vote or floor vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it a violation of consumer law for companies to write binding mandatory arbitration clauses into standard consumer contracts — credit cards, loans, phone service, purchases, and financial products. Such clauses would be unenforceable and treated as an unfair and deceptive trade practice, keeping consumers' right to take disputes to court. Arbitration would remain available, but only after a dispute actually arose and the consumer agreed to it knowingly. The bill was referred to the House Banking Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who sign standardized contracts — cardholders, borrowers, phone and utility customers, buyers of goods and services — who currently give up their day in court when they sign. The bill would let them sue in court, including joining class actions, instead of being funneled into a private arbitration process that companies choose and that studies have shown favors repeat-player businesses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers signing standard service and credit contracts

how_it_helps.text: Makes any binding arbitration clause in a consumer transaction or consumer contract unenforceable and treats it as an unfair and deceptive trade practice under federal or state law.

Covers all consumer transactions for personal, family, or household purposes, including credit extensions and financial products — so it reaches credit cards, loans, and everyday service contracts, and applies to every individual.
Preserves arbitration only for agreements made after a dispute has actually arisen, so companies cannot take the choice away in the fine print before anything goes wrong.
Applies to contracts entered into or amended after enactment and to disputes filed or arising after enactment, so it would govern real pending cases.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers, consumer lenders, and other companies that sell through standardized contracts would lose the arbitration clause, their main tool for keeping customer disputes out of court and out of class actions. Litigation defense costs for those companies would likely rise, and arbitration firms would lose a large volume of consumer business.
analysis.who_pays_short: Card issuers, lenders, and arbitration firms

drawbacks.text: The bill sweeps very broadly: it defines a consumer as any individual and covers any personal-purpose transaction, so it could reach far beyond the mass-market credit contracts that motivated it.

A good-faith objection the bill's supporters had to answer: for small-dollar individual disputes, arbitration can be faster and cheaper than court, and class actions often return little to each consumer while paying their lawyers — so a blanket ban trades one kind of access for another. The bill offered no carve-out or study process to test that trade-off.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: keeping arbitration out of the fine print restores consumers' ability to sue and join class actions, but it also means some small individual disputes may become more expensive to pursue and cost companies more to defend. The bill's main weakness is its breadth — a more targeted version limited to credit and standardized mass contracts would have addressed the same harm with less sweep. The larger problem is that the version that died was the only version Congress ever seriously weighed in this session.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: referred to the House Banking and Financial Services Committee, then to its Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit subcommittee, and no markup or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Luis Gutierrez introduced the bill on June 17, 1999, with five original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Banking and Financial Services the day it was introduced.
On July 15, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit — the last action ever taken on the bill.
Twenty-two members cosponsored the bill: 21 Democrats and 1 Independent. No Republican cosponsored, and the committee never took it up.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers, consumer lenders, and arbitration providers, who kept the ability to enforce mandatory arbitration clauses in consumer contracts for another Congress.

for.name: Rep. Luis Gutierrez

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it its full roster of 22 supporters alongside one Independent.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the chamber's only Independent supporter.

against.name: House Committee on Banking and Financial Services
against.role: Committee of referral, never took up the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on June 17, 1999, referred it to a subcommittee on July 15, and never held a markup or vote for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's lone Independent; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-led Banking Committee never scheduled the bill.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders
industries.note: These companies write binding arbitration clauses into cardholder and loan agreements, routing customer disputes into a private process they pay for and control. The bill would make those clauses unenforceable and restore consumers' access to court and class actions.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers (private arbitration firms and administrator organizations)
industries.note: Consumer arbitration clauses are their core business: companies designate the forum and pay the arbitrators. A ban on mandatory consumer arbitration would eliminate a large share of that volume.

industries.industry: Telecom, retail, and service companies selling through standardized contracts
industries.note: These firms rely on boilerplate arbitration terms to contain customer lawsuits. The bill would bar those terms in any consumer transaction, forcing disputes into the courts.
